doc.title: Vince DiMartino interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 8, 2025

title: Practicing technique and music together: Baroque recital and the racing engine
summary: He describes practicing before the call, the Bonneville engine analogy, and demonstrates phrasing over mechanics.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Lips, teeth and breath: the physical craft of brass playing

blocks.x: When we’re done here, are you going to go practice?

Do you know what I was doing when you came on? I was doing this, which is what I did last night. I played a Baroque Trumpet Recital, a 19th century recital. And I don’t play this a lot, you know. So I was playing mostly the low parts and they were playing the moving parts. Now I said, “You know I should really learn to play this more,” because I was playing the cornet solos at the end too. There were four of us. So we played baroque trumpet pieces for four baroque trumpets. I said, “Look, I can’t play the real hard parts,” I said, “’Cause I don’t really practice that that much.” So as soon as I got home I said, “Man” — I practiced it for that recital and everything. And I said, “Gee I should be able —” so I was practicing this. First you play the harmonic series to know where you are. 1:24:35 out — trumpet playing 1:34:54 in

You cannot practice music without practicing technique. You cannot practice technique without practicing music. See because I was doing like a lip slur exercise, you know they call them lip slurs, they’re really tongue slurs. But I was thinking about what it’s supposed to sound like to the audience. See? But at the same time when I’m practicing I’m finally tuning my engine. You know my brother raced cars at Bonneville Salt Flats. He built the cars. And you know he’d go out there every year and he’d come back and I’d say, “How was it?” You know. “How’d you do?” He said, “Well you know I’m up to like one-ninety-something now, (in the class he was in). I said, “Did you, you didn’t win?” He goes, “Oh no.” He says, “the guy that won, he was like almost 208 to 209. He was somewhere in there.” I said, “Aw you’ll be able to get that by next year.” He goes, “No.” He says, “Do you realize how much work it takes to go up just half a mile an hour?” And people that are discerning builders of engines, cars, suspensions, you know, alignment and everything. He says, “I might someday get close to that.” Right. And I said, “Steve,” I said, “this is just like trumpet playing.” I said, “It’s great. I’m going to use that.” I did, I used it in classes you know when I taught master classes you know and stuff. But it’s true.
